rows.claim_text: Modern Large Language Models (LLMs) predominantly use some variant of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers in their architecture, including Gemini-2.5-Pro.
rows.cited_work: [11] Gemini-Team (2025). Gemini 2.5: pushing the frontier with advanced reasoning, multimodality, long context, and next generation agentic capabilities. arXiv:2507.06261
rows.note: Cited as evidence that Gemini-2.5-Pro is a MoE LLM. Gemini 2.5 tech report is public on arXiv; whether it explicitly confirms MoE is the question.
rows.rationale: The Gemini 2.5 technical report (arXiv:2507.06261) is the canonical primary source for the Gemini 2.5-Pro model and explicitly describes its sparse MoE architecture. Using it as evidence that Gemini-2.5-Pro is a MoE LLM is a direct, on-point citation.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Gemini 2.5 technical report documents a sparse mixture-of-experts decoder backbone for the Pro tier.

rows.claim_text: Once the total number of experts outgrows GPU memory, weights must be offloaded to host memory or disk and loaded on demand.
rows.cited_work: [8] Eliseev & Mazur (2023). Fast inference of mixture-of-experts language models with offloading. arXiv:2312.17238
rows.note: Citation 8 is the canonical offloading paper for MoE LLMs.
rows.rationale: Eliseev & Mazur 2023 (arXiv:2312.17238) is exactly the foundational paper on fast MoE inference via expert offloading to host memory under GPU-memory constraints. The cited work directly substantiates the claim that offloading is the mechanism used when experts outgrow GPU memory.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Eliseev & Mazur: 'Fast inference of mixture-of-experts language models with offloading' -- weights are offloaded to host memory and prefetched per token.

rows.claim_text: Scaling the number of experts could potentially come with gains in capabilities.
rows.cited_work: [5] Clark et al. (2022). Unified scaling laws for routed language models. ICML.
rows.note: Routed scaling-laws paper studies the effect of expert count on capability.
rows.rationale: Clark et al. 2022 'Unified scaling laws for routed language models' is exactly a paper deriving capability gains from scaling expert count in routed (MoE) LMs. Direct support.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Clark et al. derive scaling laws showing that increasing the number of experts (routed parameters) yields capability gains at fixed compute, validating the cited claim.

rows.claim_text: Choosing when to commit to a set of resources and when to pay the cost of switching is exactly the structure formalized by temporally extended actions in the options framework.
rows.cited_work: [35] Sutton, Precup & Singh (1999). Between MDPs and semi-MDPs: a framework for temporal abstraction in reinforcement learning. Artificial Intelligence 112(1).
rows.note: Foundational options-framework paper. Should clearly support the claim.
rows.rationale: Sutton, Precup & Singh (1999) is THE canonical reference for the options framework / temporally extended actions in semi-MDPs. The claim cites it exactly for what the paper introduced.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Sutton, Precup, Singh (1999), 'Between MDPs and semi-MDPs', formalizes options as temporally extended actions that persist over multiple time steps.

rows.claim_text: Switching to a new option incurs a deliberation cost.
rows.cited_work: [14] Harb, Bacon, Klissarov & Precup (2017). When waiting is not an option: learning options with a deliberation cost. arXiv:1709.04571
rows.note: Paper title itself is about deliberation cost.
rows.rationale: Harb, Bacon, Klissarov & Precup 2017 'When waiting is not an option: learning options with a deliberation cost' is explicitly about adding deliberation costs to option switching. The claim is an exact restatement of the paper's contribution.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Harb et al. introduce a deliberation cost term penalizing option termination/switching in the option-critic objective.

rows.claim_text: The controller is optimized via the option-critic architecture with deliberation costs.
rows.cited_work: [1] Bacon, Harb & Precup (2016). The option-critic architecture. arXiv:1609.05140
rows.note: Origin paper for option-critic.
rows.rationale: Bacon, Harb & Precup 2016 (arXiv:1609.05140) is the original option-critic paper. Citing it as the source of the option-critic architecture is direct support.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Bacon, Harb, Precup derive policy-gradient theorems for options and propose the option-critic architecture.

rows.section: §3.1 Current MoEs are not temporally extended
rows.claim_text: We measure the switch rate of three frontier open-source MoE models -- gpt-oss-20b (32 experts, top-4), gpt-oss-120b (128 experts, top-4), and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B (512 experts, top-10) -- on 100 prompts from each of the 10 categories in the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset v2.
rows.cited_work: [26] Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 (no author/year listed in references)
rows.note: Citation has no proper author/year and is just a Link. Existence of the dataset on HF should be checkable.
rows.rationale: The Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 is a real NVIDIA-released dataset on Hugging Face, so the citation exists in artefact form. However, the reference list entry has NO author, NO year, and only a 'Link' field, which means the citation is bibliographically incomplete and not independently verifiable by the standard citation hygiene tests a reviewer would apply. The dataset itself does support the claim of providing 10 categories of prompts.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Nemotron-Post-Training-Dataset-v2 on Hugging Face contains multi-domain SFT/RL prompts grouped into category subsets; the artefact exists, but the bibliographic record in the paper is stub-like.

rows.claim_text: [40] presents MoE-infinity that offloads certain experts to host memory and allows memory-constrained GPUs to serve MoE models. It uses expert activations to predict the set of experts to cache and prefetch.
rows.cited_work: [40] Xue, Fu, Lu, Mai & Marina (2025). MoE-Infinity: efficient MoE inference on personal machines with sparsity-aware expert cache. arXiv:2401.14361
rows.note: Detailed characterization of the cited work; very specific.
rows.rationale: Xue et al. 2024/2025 'MoE-Infinity' (arXiv:2401.14361) is exactly the paper that designs an offloading-aware MoE serving system with sparsity-aware expert caching driven by activation history. The body text's characterization is accurate.
rows.evidence_excerpt: MoE-Infinity uses past activation traces to maintain a sparsity-aware expert cache and prefetch policy for memory-constrained MoE inference.

rows.claim_text: [4] frames sequence of tokens as macro-actions and incorporates them into RLHF.
rows.cited_work: [4] Chai, Sun, Fang, Wang, Sun, Wu (2025). MA-RLHF: reinforcement learning from human feedback with macro actions. arXiv:2410.02743
rows.note: Title matches the characterization.
rows.rationale: Chai et al. 2024 'MA-RLHF' (arXiv:2410.02743) does exactly what the body text claims: introduces macro-actions over token sequences into RLHF. Direct support.
rows.evidence_excerpt: MA-RLHF treats contiguous spans of tokens as macro-actions and applies RLHF over the macro-action policy rather than per-token.

rows.claim_text: Some works apply expert pruning to reduce the total number of experts by permanently removing or merging experts, possibly with additional fine-tuning [39, 24, 25].
rows.cited_work: [25] Muzio, Sun & He (2024). SEER-MoE: sparse expert efficiency through regularization for mixture-of-experts. arXiv:2404.05089
rows.note: Worth checking: SEER-MoE applies regularization-based sparsity rather than the kind of explicit prune-then-finetune the body text describes.
rows.rationale: SEER-MoE (Muzio, Sun, He 2024) does address MoE efficiency by reducing the effective number of active experts via regularization toward sparsity, which is *related to* expert pruning but not literally 'permanently removing or merging experts'. The body text's framing as straightforward prune-then-finetune slightly mischaracterizes SEER-MoE's mechanism (regularization-driven sparsity) -- partial support at best.
rows.evidence_excerpt: SEER-MoE applies a heavy-hitter-counting heuristic + regularization to push routing toward fewer experts; it does not strictly 'remove' experts the way [24] and [39] do.

rows.claim_text: Large language models (LLMs) are typically trained and deployed as monolithic systems: a single model is pretrained, finetuned, and served as one unified entity [1, 2, 3].
rows.cited_work: [1] Team Olmo et al. (2026). Olmo 3.
rows.note: Olmo 3 is itself a model release, not necessarily about the *monolithic deployment paradigm* per se. May be a weak/illustrative citation rather than direct support.
rows.rationale: The claim is about the *monolithic-deployment paradigm* of LLMs; Olmo 3 is itself just a recent monolithic LLM release. Olmo 3 is therefore at best a tangential illustration -- the citation is to an instance, not to evidence that the paradigm exists or has the listed drawbacks. The citation is meant illustratively (a list of three model releases [1,2,3]) but in isolation [1] does not establish anything about the paradigm itself.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Olmo 3 is a model release artefact (weights + tech report); it is an example of monolithic deployment rather than a study of monolithic deployment.

rows.claim_text: DeepSeek-V3 employs hundreds of experts per layer while activating only a small subset per token -- allowing models to reach scales of hundreds of billions of parameters.
rows.cited_work: [2] DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025). DeepSeek-V3 technical report.
rows.note: DeepSeek-V3 tech report should clearly contain expert counts.
rows.rationale: The DeepSeek-V3 technical report explicitly documents 256 routed experts per MoE layer with 8 active per token, totaling 671B parameters with 37B active. The claim is directly substantiated by the cited work.
rows.evidence_excerpt: DeepSeek-V3 reports 256 routed + 1 shared expert per layer, 8 active per token, 671B total / 37B active parameters.

rows.claim_text: This has motivated a line of work such as memory-constrained scaling laws [14].
rows.cited_work: [14] Li, Lo, Wang, Wang, Zheng, Zhou, Zhang, Jiang. Can mixture-of-experts surpass dense LLMs under strictly equal resources? ICLR 2026.
rows.note: Title is about dense vs MoE under equal resources, not necessarily 'memory-constrained scaling laws' specifically. Possible mismatch between citation framing and cited work content.
rows.rationale: Li et al. 'Can mixture-of-experts surpass dense LLMs under strictly equal resources?' (ICLR 2026) is about the dense-vs-MoE comparison at fixed compute/parameter budget, NOT specifically about 'memory-constrained scaling laws'. The cited work's framing centers on equal-resource comparison, not memory as the binding constraint. Naming it 'memory-constrained scaling laws' overstates and slightly mischaracterizes the cited contribution.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Li et al. study under-what-conditions MoE matches dense LLMs at equal training compute/parameters; the work is a fair-compute comparison study, not a memory-axis scaling-law paper.

rows.claim_text: Prior work finds that specialization is often driven by surface-level patterns (e.g., token ID that is context-independent) or low-level lexical cues (e.g., prepositions, punctuations) [16, 17].
rows.cited_work: [16] Jiang et al. (2024). Mixtral of experts. arXiv:2401.04088
rows.note: Mixtral paper has expert-specialization analysis; question is whether its conclusions match the claim's framing.
rows.rationale: The Mixtral paper (Jiang et al. 2024) does include an expert-specialization analysis and reports that observed specialization correlates more with surface/positional patterns than with semantic domains. So it partly supports the claim. However, the more famous and specific finding about token-ID-driven specialization is from other follow-up analyses; Mixtral itself reports the negative finding more in passing than as a central result. Partial support is the most honest verdict.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Mixtral's appendix routing analysis shows little evidence of high-level domain specialization and notes correlations with token-ID-like surface patterns.

rows.claim_text: Other work suggests that apparent expert specialization may largely reflect geometric properties of the representation space that is difficult to interpret [19].
rows.cited_work: [19] Wang, Hayou & Nalisnick. The myth of expert specialization in MoEs: why routing reflects geometry, not necessarily domain expertise. arXiv:2604.09780
rows.note: Title is essentially the same claim.
rows.rationale: Wang, Hayou & Nalisnick 'The myth of expert specialization in MoEs: why routing reflects geometry, not necessarily domain expertise' (arXiv:2604.09780) makes exactly the claim that apparent specialization reflects representation-space geometry. The cited work is a near-verbatim source for the claim.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Wang, Hayou, Nalisnick argue that MoE routing decisions follow geometric structure of token embeddings rather than encoding interpretable domain-level expertise.

rows.claim_text: We address this by adopting global load balancing [31], aggregating routing statistics across data-parallel groups.
rows.cited_work: [31] Qiu et al. (2025). Demons in the detail: on implementing load balancing loss for training specialized mixture-of-expert models. ACL.
rows.note: Title aligns with load-balancing implementation details.
rows.rationale: Qiu et al. 'Demons in the detail: on implementing load balancing loss for training specialized MoE models' (ACL 2025) is exactly about correct load-balancing implementations -- in particular, the global vs. local (data-parallel) aggregation question that the EMO paper invokes here. The citation maps to the cited work's central finding.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Qiu et al. analyze how load-balance loss aggregation across data-parallel groups affects expert specialization and training stability, advocating global aggregation.

rows.claim_text: We train both the baseline MoE and EMO from scratch on 1 trillion tokens from the OLMoE pretraining corpus.
rows.cited_work: [17] Muennighoff et al. (2025). OLMoE: open mixture-of-experts language models. ICLR.
rows.note: OLMoE paper documents its pretraining corpus.
rows.rationale: Muennighoff et al. OLMoE (ICLR 2025) documents the pretraining corpus used to train OLMoE. EMO using 'the OLMoE pretraining corpus' is correctly attributed.
rows.evidence_excerpt: OLMoE technical report describes its 5T-token pretraining corpus composition (DCLM, Dolma, etc.).

rows.claim_text: Another line of work explicitly partitions training data into predefined domains (e.g., math, biomedical), train separate experts, and merge them into a single MoE [7, 6, 28].
rows.cited_work: [6] Sukhbaatar et al. (2024). Branch-Train-MiX: mixing expert LLMs into a mixture-of-experts LLM. COLM.
rows.note: Branch-Train-MiX is the canonical 'partition + merge into MoE' approach.
rows.rationale: Branch-Train-MiX (Sukhbaatar et al. 2024) is the canonical 'partition data into domains, train experts separately, merge into one MoE' method. Direct support for the claim.
rows.evidence_excerpt: BTX trains separate dense experts on domain-specific data (math, code, etc.) then merges them with router-style mixing into a single MoE.

rows.claim_text: The closest line of work is ModuleFormer [29], which shares our goal of training a modular MoE that supports standalone use of expert subsets.
rows.cited_work: [29] Shen, Zhang, Cao, Tan, Chen & Gan (2023). ModuleFormer: modularity emerges from mixture-of-experts.
rows.note: Title clearly aligns.
rows.rationale: ModuleFormer (Shen et al. 2023) is explicitly about training modular MoE expert subsets that can be used standalone via a mutual-information objective. Direct support for the characterization as 'closest line of work'.
rows.evidence_excerpt: ModuleFormer trains experts with a mutual-information objective so subsets remain functional in isolation, identical in spirit to EMO's modularity goal.

rows.claim_text: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are decoder-only Transformer language models in which the feedforward sublayer is replaced by a sparse mixture of expert networks.
rows.cited_work: [30] Vaswani et al. (2017). Attention is all you need. NeurIPS.
rows.note: Vaswani 2017 introduced the Transformer but did NOT introduce MoE or even decoder-only design. Citation may be tangential to the specific MoE-replaces-FFN claim.
rows.rationale: The claim concerns the specific architectural choice that 'decoder-only Transformer language models replace the feedforward sublayer with a sparse MoE'. Vaswani et al. 2017 'Attention is all you need' introduced the encoder-decoder Transformer but (a) did not introduce decoder-only LMs and (b) did not introduce MoE. The closest correct primary citations would be Radford et al. (GPT, for decoder-only) and Shazeer et al. 2017 (for FFN-replacement-by-MoE, which is reference [11] in this paper). Citing Vaswani for an MoE-replaces-FFN-in-decoder-only-Transformer claim is a weak/illustrative citation rather than direct support.
rows.evidence_excerpt: Vaswani et al. 2017 introduce the Transformer encoder-decoder with attention + dense feedforward; the paper neither defines decoder-only LMs nor introduces mixture-of-experts.
